body:
What did the early Congress demand?

The early Congress sought to increase Indian participation in government, reduce economic hardship and protect civil rights.

Its demands were linked by a common argument: government policies affecting Indians should not be decided without giving Indians a meaningful opportunity to express their views.

During the Moderate phase, the Congress generally sought reforms within the existing political system rather than demanding immediate and complete independence.

Major demands of the Moderates

AreaPrincipal demandReason
Legislative councilsMore Indian representatives and greater powersIncrease public participation in government
Civil servicesGreater Indian recruitment and examinations in IndiaReduce discriminatory exclusion from administration
Judicial administrationSeparation of the judiciary from the executiveImprove impartiality in judicial decisions
Civil rightsFreedom of speech and repeal of discriminatory restrictionsProtect political expression and equal treatment
Public expenditureReduction of excessive military and administrative spendingRelease resources for public needs
Land revenueReduction of burdensome revenue demandsRelieve economic pressure on cultivators
Public welfareGreater expenditure on irrigation and public improvementsSupport agriculture and reduce hardship

Reform of legislative councils

The Moderates demanded that the legislative councils should become more representative and possess greater powers.

Legislative councils were institutions through which certain laws and public matters could be discussed. However, their membership and powers under colonial rule were restricted, and officials retained substantial control over decisions.

The Congress wanted greater Indian representation and a more meaningful role for representatives in examining government policies and expenditure.

This was an important constitutional demand because it questioned the principle that colonial officials could govern India without effective public accountability.

Indianisation of the civil services

Important administrative positions in British India were dominated by Europeans. One reason was that access to the higher civil services was difficult for Indian candidates.

The Indian Civil Service examination was conducted in Britain, placing Indian candidates at a disadvantage because of travel costs, distance and other barriers.

The Moderates therefore demanded that civil service examinations should be held simultaneously in India and Britain.

They also sought greater appointment of qualified Indians to important administrative positions.

This demand had 2 connected purposes. It sought to reduce racial discrimination in government employment and increase Indian influence over administrative decisions.

Nationalist leaders also argued that employing more Indians could reduce the amount of official salaries and savings transferred from India to Britain.

Indianisation of services meant increasing the participation of Indians in government employment, particularly higher positions. It was not the same as obtaining complete Indian control over the colonial government.

Separation of the judiciary from the executive

The Moderates demanded a clearer separation between judicial and executive functions.

Under colonial administrative arrangements, some officials exercised both executive authority and judicial powers. This combination could weaken judicial independence because an official responsible for administering government policy might also exercise authority in deciding cases.

Separation of the judiciary from the executive meant ensuring that judicial decisions were made independently of officials responsible for ordinary executive administration.

The demand was intended to promote impartial justice and reduce the possibility of administrative influence over judicial decisions.

Freedom of expression and equal treatment

The early nationalists criticised restrictions on political speech and publications. They argued that Indians should be able to discuss government policies and express grievances without discriminatory interference.

They also demanded repeal of the Arms Act and opposed racial discrimination in government institutions.

The controversy surrounding the Ilbert Bill had already demonstrated that legal qualifications did not necessarily ensure equal treatment for Indian and European officials.

Economic and welfare demands

The Congress raised several economic issues affecting ordinary Indians, even though its early membership was dominated by educated urban groups.

  • Land revenue: It demanded relief from burdensome revenue demands imposed on cultivators.
  • Military expenditure: It criticised excessive expenditure that placed pressure on Indian public finances.
  • Irrigation: It demanded greater expenditure on irrigation and improvements useful to agriculture.
  • Salt tax: It criticised taxation that increased the cost of an essential commodity.
  • Other grievances: It raised concerns about the treatment of Indian labourers abroad and the hardships caused by restrictive forest administration.

These demands show that the Congress's political programme was not restricted to government jobs or the interests of educated professionals. Nevertheless, discussing the difficulties of peasants and workers did not necessarily mean that those groups were adequately represented within the Congress organisation.

The Indian Councils Act, 1892

One important constitutional development during the Moderate phase was the Indian Councils Act of 1892.

The Act expanded the membership of legislative councils and introduced limited opportunities for greater non-official participation.

It also permitted members to discuss the annual budget without voting on it or moving financial resolutions and to ask questions concerning public administration, normally with 6 clear days' notice; supplementary questions were not allowed.

What did the Act permit?

  • Expansion in the number of additional members of legislative councils.
  • Limited indirect representation through arrangements in which designated bodies could recommend members for nomination.
  • Discussion of the annual budget without voting on it or moving financial resolutions.
  • Questions on administrative matters, normally with 6 clear days' notice and without supplementary questions.

What did the Act not provide?

  • It did not establish direct elections based on a general popular vote.
  • It did not give legislative councils the power to vote on and approve the budget.
  • It did not establish an executive government responsible to elected Indian representatives.
  • It did not transfer effective control of colonial administration to Indians.

The Act represented a limited constitutional concession, but it fell substantially short of nationalist demands for genuinely representative government.

The expansion of council powers should therefore not be confused with parliamentary self-government.

Discussion is not decision-making authority

Under the Indian Councils Act of 1892, members could discuss the budget under restricted conditions, but they could not vote on it. Greater opportunity to express criticism did not amount to control over public expenditure.

Prelims focus

  • Moderates demanded greater Indian representation in legislative councils.
  • They sought simultaneous civil service examinations in India and Britain.
  • They demanded separation of the judiciary from the executive.
  • Economic demands included lower land revenue, reduced military expenditure and more irrigation spending.
  • The Indian Councils Act was enacted in 1892.
  • The Act allowed restricted budget discussion and questions but not voting on the budget.
  • Trap: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 did not establish direct popular elections or responsible government.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, A Nation in the Making, printed pp. 111–112; President of India, History of Parliamentary Democracy in India, memorial lecture delivered on 15 May 2017, paragraphs 19–22 concerning the Indian Councils Act of 1892, consulted 20 November 2026; Indian National Congress, Brief History of Congress, entry concerning the 1892 Allahabad session, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Powers and limitations of legislative councils under the Act of 1892.

title: Political, Administrative and Economic Demands of the Early Congress

body:
Why did economic questions become central to nationalism?

Economic criticism was among the most important contributions of the early Indian nationalists.

Many educated Indians had initially believed that British rule might promote economic development through modern administration, transport and trade. However, nationalist economic thinkers increasingly argued that the structure of colonial rule subordinated India's economic interests to those of Britain.

They examined land-revenue policies, public expenditure, trade patterns, industrial decline and the movement of income from India to Britain.

By connecting these issues, the early nationalists developed a broader argument: India's poverty could not be explained only by local conditions because important economic decisions were controlled by a foreign government.

Dadabhai Naoroji and the Drain of Wealth Theory

Dadabhai Naoroji developed the influential Drain of Wealth Theory, which explained how a portion of India's income and resources was transferred to Britain without an equivalent economic return to India.

He argued that colonial administration created continuing payments and transfers that reduced the resources available for India's own economic development.

Naoroji used economic statistics, trade information and government financial records to support his arguments.

His important work Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, published in 1901, brought together his criticism of the economic consequences of British rule.

Drain of wealth

The drain of wealth refers to the transfer of economic resources from colonial India to Britain without an equivalent return in goods, services or benefits to India. Nationalist economists argued that such transfers weakened India's capacity to save, invest and develop its economy.

How did the drain of wealth occur?

Remittances by European officials

European officials employed in India received salaries from Indian government revenues. Some transferred their savings and earnings to Britain or spent them on supporting families living there.

Nationalist economists argued that these transfers moved income generated or collected in India outside the Indian economy.

Pensions and overseas administrative expenditure

Certain pensions and administrative expenses connected with British rule were paid in Britain from revenues associated with India.

These payments formed part of the wider financial relationship that nationalists criticised.

Interest and other financial obligations

Payments of interest on certain government debts and other financial obligations could also transfer resources abroad.

Nationalist criticism focused particularly on obligations created or maintained under colonial control and paid from Indian resources.

Home Charges

The expression Home Charges referred to expenditures connected with the government of India that were payable in Britain.

Such expenditure included administrative and financial obligations associated with colonial rule.

Nationalist thinkers considered these payments an important channel through which Indian resources were used outside India.

Drain of wealth and ordinary international trade

The distinction between the drain of wealth and ordinary international trade is important.

When a country exports goods and receives payment of equivalent value, an ordinary commercial exchange occurs. The exporter receives financial resources in return for the goods.

The nationalist criticism concerned situations in which Indian resources were transferred abroad without an equivalent economic benefit returning to India.

For example, an export surplus would not necessarily indicate national prosperity if its proceeds were used to meet colonial government's financial obligations in Britain rather than adding to resources available within India.

The essential question was therefore not simply whether India exported more than it imported, but how the resulting financial claims and proceeds were used.

Exports are not automatically a drain of wealth. The economic criticism concerned the transfer of resources without an equivalent return. Colonial financial obligations and overseas payments were central to the nationalist argument.

The decline of traditional industries

Nationalist economists also criticised the impact of British trade and industrial policies on Indian manufacturing.

Before British political dominance, India possessed important textile, handicraft and other manufacturing industries.

During colonial rule, India increasingly supplied raw materials to Britain and imported manufactured products from British industries.

Traditional Indian producers faced competition from machine-made imports and other disadvantages. The weakening of traditional manufacturing activities is commonly described as deindustrialisation.

Deindustrialisation

Deindustrialisation refers to the decline or weakening of industrial and manufacturing activity. In the context of colonial India, it is especially associated with the decline of traditional handicrafts and manufacturing under changing colonial economic conditions.

Deindustrialisation did not mean that every form of Indian industry disappeared. Modern cotton textile mills also developed in parts of western India, including Maharashtra and Gujarat, during the colonial period.

The nationalist argument was that the overall structure of colonial trade and industrial policy failed to promote Indian economic development adequately and placed important sectors at a disadvantage.

Land revenue, agriculture and poverty

Land-revenue policies were another important subject of nationalist criticism.

High revenue demands could reduce cultivators' income and leave them with fewer resources for agricultural improvement or protection against crop failures.

Nationalists also criticised inadequate expenditure on irrigation and the vulnerability of agriculture to poor harvests.

The early Congress argued that colonial policies had contributed to poverty and famine conditions. It particularly objected to heavy land-revenue demands and the export of food grains during periods when people faced severe hardship.

These were important arguments advanced by nationalist leaders. The occurrence and severity of individual famines also depended on factors such as rainfall failure, food availability, purchasing power and administrative responses.

Romesh Chandra Dutt and the economic history of colonial India

Romesh Chandra Dutt, also known as R. C. Dutt, was another important nationalist economic thinker.

He examined the history of British economic administration in India, with particular attention to agriculture, land revenue and the effects of colonial policies.

His work The Economic History of India contributed to the argument that British economic policies had damaged Indian economic interests.

Dutt especially criticised the burden of land revenue and its effects on agricultural society.

While Naoroji is most closely associated with the Drain of Wealth Theory, Dutt is particularly associated with the historical examination of colonial economic administration and agrarian conditions.

Mahadev Govind Ranade and Indian industrial development

Mahadev Govind Ranade also contributed to nationalist economic thought.

He emphasised the importance of industrial development and argued for measures that could strengthen India's productive economy.

His concern with industrial growth complemented the wider nationalist criticism of economic policies that favoured British commercial interests.

Why the economic critique mattered politically

The early economic nationalists helped transform economic grievances into political arguments.

They connected poverty, public expenditure and trade policies with the broader question of who controlled economic decisions.

Their arguments also helped explain why increasing Indian participation in government was important. If Indians possessed greater influence over expenditure and economic policy, nationalists argued, government resources could be directed more effectively towards Indian needs.

This established an important connection between economic criticism and the demand for political representation.

The Gujarat connection

Dadabhai Naoroji's association with Bombay and Gujarati Parsi society provides an important regional connection to early economic nationalism.

Gujarat was also part of the western Indian region where modern cotton textile manufacturing developed during colonial rule.

The existence of textile mills in Gujarat illustrates an important distinction: nationalist criticism of deindustrialisation concerned the decline and disadvantages of important Indian industries, particularly traditional manufacturing, rather than the complete absence of industrial development.

Prelims focus

  • Drain of Wealth Theory: Dadabhai Naoroji.
  • Poverty and Un-British Rule in India: Dadabhai Naoroji, 1901.
  • Home Charges: expenditures connected with Indian administration payable in Britain.
  • Romesh Chandra Dutt: economic history, land revenue and colonial economic policies.
  • Mahadev Govind Ranade: Indian industrial development and economic reform.
  • Deindustrialisation: decline or weakening of manufacturing, particularly traditional industries.
  • Trap: A trade surplus is not automatically evidence that the exporting country is retaining the proceeds for its own development.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, A Nation in the Making, printed pp. 111–112; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 1, Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence, printed pp. 4–9, sections 1.2–1.5; Press Information Bureau, Dadabhai Naoroji: The Man Who Brought Statistics into Politics, 27 June 2017, consulted 20 November 2026; Dadabhai Naoroji, Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, 1901, discussion of the economic drain; Reserve Bank of India, RBI Bulletin, discussion of Naoroji's Drain Theory and nationalist economic thought, consulted 20 November 2026.]
